text: 43 Facilities and How to Choose Them Acceleration Measurement and Environment Characterization The terms microgravity, reduced gravity, low gravity, zero gravity and weightlessness are often used interchangeably to describe an environment where the gravitational body force is significantly less than that on Earth. This ambiguous description points to a question of how to measure and characterize a reduced-gravity environment and any disturbances. Disturbances in a microgravity environment are created by crew activities such as exercising, push-offs and landings, and simply opening and closing drawers and doors in addition to equipment operation, vehicle docking and undocking, thruster firings, and other movements. These disturbances must be measured to understand their impact on the data from scientific and engineering experiments. The Space Acceleration Measurement System (SAMS) and the Microgravity Acceleration Measurement System (MAMS) provide continuous measurement of the ISS vibratory and quasi-steady acceleration environment, respectively. SAMS sensors measure acceleration levels using tri-axis accelerometers. SAMS flew on Mir from 1994 to 1998, continued on 20 shuttle missions and currently flies aboard the ISS. To complement SAMS, MAMS was developed to measure the very low-frequency disturbances (less than 0.01 hertz) that the SAMS sensors are unable to detect.

text: First Apollo Mission Commences In November 1966, after the successful completion of the Gemini program, NASA turned its focus to the first Apollo mission to carry a crew to the Moon. The mission, officially designated as AS-204, later became known as Apollo 1. NASA planned the mission as an open-ended flight lasting up to 14 days and targeted a launch for the first quarter of 1967. The main goals were to prove the space worthiness of the craft and test the Service Module’s large engine. Apollo I Construction Following two uncrewed suborbital tests of the Apollo spacecraft in 1966, AS-204 was to be the first Block I to carry astronauts into Earth orbit. Construction of Command Module (CM) 012, the spacecraft assigned to AS-204, began in Downey, California, in August 1964. Apollo I Crew NASA assigned Mercury 4 and Gemini 3 veteran Virgil “Gus” Grissom, Gemini IV veteran and the first American to conduct a spacewalk Edward White, and spaceflight rookie Roger Chaffee, as the crew for the Apollo I mission.

text: ## 25 Years Ago: Fire Aboard Space Station Mir Article On Feb. 24, 1997, the six crew members aboard the Russian space station Mir faced significant danger when a fire ignited in an oxygen generating system. The searing flame, lasting several minutes, not only cut off access to one of the two Soyuz escape vehicles but also filled the station’s modules with smoke. Although the narrow confines where the fire occurred made fighting it difficult, through teamwork and composure the crew prevailed and extinguished the flames, with no damage to the station’s structure. The station’s life support systems cleared its atmosphere of the toxic smoke over several hours, with no lasting harm to the crew members. The lessons learned from the incident were passed on in the design and operations of the International Space Station. text: ## New Technology for the Fire Attire Although little can be done to reduce the risks of firefighting, something can be done to curb the injuries and fatalities. This is the goal of Project FIRES, a program jointly sponsored by NASA and the Federal Emergency Management Agency's U.S. Fire Administration with technical management provided by Marshall Space Flight Center. Project FIRES (Firefighter's Integrated Response Equipment System) involves applications of advanced materials and design concepts, derived from Apollo to update existing gear which does not adequately protect against many of the hazards encountered in fire suppression activities. A major focus of the effort involves application to the FIRES ensemble of lightweight, fire-resistant, heat-protective materials originally developed for use in astronauts' space suits or in spacecraft components which require thermal protection. Data from the fourteen municipal fire departments participating in the field evaluation will form a basis for development of new nationwide protective ensemble students. title: Flame in Freefall challenge statement
text: Why flames differ in microgravity: In microgravity there is no buoyancy, so hot gases do not rise. Instead of a flickering teardrop, a candle flame becomes a blue sphere that relies on diffusion for its oxygen. Air flow is therefore important for flammability in microgravity.

title: Flame in Freefall challenge statement
text: NASA fire-safety strategy: NASA's spacecraft fire safety work focuses on prevention, detection and suppression. Prevention comes from controlling ignition sources and selecting materials, which depends on understanding flammability limits. Flammability depends strongly on oxygen concentration, and air flow also matters in microgravity. Solid materials such as fabrics and plastics were studied in BASS, BASS-II and Saffire-I, -II and -III. Fire detection was tested through SAME and SAME-R. Suppression was studied in FLEX by diluting the chamber atmosphere with carbon dioxide and helium.

title: Flame in Freefall challenge statement
text: Moon base oxygen and pressure: Spacesuits are filled with 100% oxygen at only 4.3 psi, while Earth's sea-level pressure is 14.7 psi. To shorten oxygen pre-breathing before moonwalks, Moon bases and pressurized rovers are expected to use a pressure and oxygen level between the two. The oxygen concentration on the Moon will likely be 30% or greater at a pressure of 10.2 psi or less: more than a 40% increase over Earth's air, making materials much more flammable.

title: Flame in Freefall challenge statement
text: Highest-oxygen microgravity tests: The microgravity tests with the highest oxygen concentrations were in ACME's Cool Flames Investigation with Gases (CFI-G): an oxygen-nitrogen mixture of up to 85% oxygen flowed from a spherical burner into a chamber of nitrogen and fuel gas, creating an inside-out flame.

title: Flame in Freefall challenge statement
text: Partial gravity: PSI holds no partial-gravity combustion data yet; it is expected from the Lunar-g Combustion Investigation (LUCI) and the Flammability of Materials on the Moon (FM2) experiment. ACME's E-FIELD Flames mimicked partial gravity using an electric field acting on the ions in flames. Microgravity and normal-gravity results could bound what happens at intermediate gravity such as on the Moon and Mars.

title: Flame in Freefall challenge statement
text: Shared hardware: The six ACME experiments burned gaseous fuels with the same modular ACME hardware in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR). FLEX, FLEX-2 and the Cool Flames Investigation burned liquid droplets in the Multi-user Droplet Combustion Apparatus (MDCA). BASS, BASS-II, SPICE and SLICE used the Microgravity Science Glovebox with the fan-driven flow duct built for SPICE.

title: Flame in Freefall challenge statement
text: Other relevant investigations: An instrument used for smoke detection in SAME and SAME-R was used to detect dust in DAFT and DAFT-2. Although it burned gaseous fuels, the ACME Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) studied the flammability of materials in still atmospheres as a function of material properties.

title: Flame in Freefall challenge statement
text: Scope and Earth applications: Rocket and propellant fires are outside the scope of PSI, because combustion at rocket-engine speeds is effectively independent of gravity. PSI data also applies on Earth: fine-water-mist extinguishers developed for the ISS have Earth uses, and NASA technology improved smoke detection and firefighter gear such as protective clothing and air tanks.

title: Flame in Freefall challenge statement
text: Real spacecraft fires: A smoke alarm went off during the Artemis II mission. Apollo 13 suffered an oxygen tank explosion on the way to the Moon. A crew survived a fire aboard the Mir space station caused by an oxygen generator failure. In 1967 the Apollo 1 crew died in a pre-launch test when fire erupted in their oxygen-filled spacecraft.
